en: The Treatise on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna, one fascicle.
Composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Western India during the Liang Dynasty.
I take refuge in those who pervade the ten directions, The most supreme ones, the omniscient,
Masters of form and unimpeded mastery, The Great Compassionate Saviors of the world;
And in their physical marks and features, The ocean of the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā-tathatā).
The treasury of immeasurable merit, such as the practice of reality as it is,
is for the sake of causing sentient beings to eliminate doubt and abandon false attachments,
to give rise to right faith in the Mahāyāna, and so that the lineage of the Buddhas shall not be severed.
The Treatise says:
There is a dharma capable of giving rise to the faculty of faith in the Mahāyāna; therefore, it should be explained.
This explanation consists of five parts.
What are the five? First, the section on causes and conditions;
second, the section on establishing the doctrine; third, the section on explanation; fourth, the section on practicing faith; and fifth, the section on the benefits of encouraging practice.
First is the section on the introduction of the causes and conditions. Question:
"For what causes and conditions was this treatise composed?"
He replied:
"There are eight kinds of such causal conditions.
What are these eight?"

First is the general characteristic of the causal conditions: namely, to cause sentient beings to leave all suffering behind and attain ultimate bliss, rather than seeking worldly fame, profit, or honor.
Second, it is because he wishes to explain the fundamental meaning of the Tathāgata, so that all sentient beings may attain correct understanding without error.
Third, it is because he wishes to enable those sentient beings whose roots of goodness are matured to become capable of non-retrogressive faith in the Mahāyāna Dharma.
Fourth, it is to cause sentient beings with meager roots of goodness to cultivate faith.

Fifth, it is to demonstrate skillful means for eliminating the obstacles of evil karma, to well protect their minds, and to lead them away from delusion and pride so they may escape the net of heterodoxy.
Sixth, it is to demonstrate the cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā as an antidote to the mental faults of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles.
Seventh, it is to demonstrate the skillful means of single-minded mindfulness so that one may be born before the Buddhas and certainly never retreat from the faith.
"Eight, it is for the purpose of demonstrating benefits and encouraging practice.
Because of such causes and conditions as these, this treatise was composed. He asked:
"If this Dharma is already contained within the Sūtras, why is it necessary to state it again?
He replied,
"Although this Dharma exists within the Sūtras, because the faculties and practices of sentient beings are unequal, and their conditions for receiving and understanding are distinct."

That is to say, when the Tathāgata was in the world, sentient beings possessed sharp faculties, the speaker’s physical and mental karma was supreme, and his perfect voice was uttered but once for all classes of beings to be understood equally; thus, there was no need for further discourse.
If, after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, there are sentient beings who are able to attain understanding through extensive hearing by means of their own power;
or there are sentient beings who likewise attain much understanding through little hearing by means of their own power;
or there are sentient beings who lack the power of their own minds and attain understanding by relying upon extensive treatises;

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who find extensive treatises cumbersome due to their great length; they delight in concise summaries that encapsulate vast meanings within few words and are capable of attaining understanding through them.
Therefore, because this treatise seeks to comprehensively summarize the boundless meanings of the Tathāgata’s vast and profound Dharma, it should be expounded.
The section on causes and conditions has been explained.
Next, the section on establishing the doctrine is explained.
Regarding the Mahāyāna, there are generally two types.
What are these two? First, the phenomena (dharma); second, their meaning (artha).
What is called "phenomena" refers to the mind of sentient beings; this mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena.
Based on this mind, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed.
Why is this? Because the aspect of the suchness of this mind reveals the very essence of the Mahāyāna.
This is the characteristic of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of the mind, which is able to demonstrate the essence, characteristics, and function of the Mahāyāna.
As for what is called "meaning," there are three kinds. What are these three?
First is the greatness of essence (*tattva-mahat*), meaning that the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena is equal, neither increasing nor decreasing.
Second is the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahat*), meaning that the tathāgatagarbha is fully endowed with immeasurable innate merits (*guṇa*).
Third, it is great in its function, for it can produce all mundane and supramundane wholesome causes and effects.
It is that which all Buddhas have fundamentally mounted, and by means of this Dharma, all Bodhisattvas reach the stage of the Tathāgata.
The section on establishing the thesis has already been explained.
Next, the section on the explanation will be discussed.
This section on the explanation consists of three parts.
What are these three?
First, the manifestation of the correct meaning; second, the counteracting of erroneous attachments; and third, the differentiation of the characteristics of those who have set out upon the path.
To elucidate the correct principle, based on the dharma of the one mind, there are two gates.
What are these two?
First, the gate of the suchness of mind; second, the gate of the arising and ceasing of mind.
These two gates each comprehensively encompass all phenomena. How is this so?
Because these two gates are not mutually exclusive.
The suchness of the mind is the essence of the Dharma-gate of the Great Universal Characteristic of the Single Dharma-realm.

That which is called the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished; all phenomena exist only through the distinctions created by deluded thoughts. If one is free from deluded thoughts, then there are no appearances of any objective realms.

Therefore, all phenomena from their very origin have been free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names and words, and free from the characteristics of mental objects; they are ultimately equal, without change or variation, and indestructible.

It is solely this one mind that is called True Suchness (*tathatā*), because all verbal expressions are merely provisional designations lacking reality; they cannot be apprehended as they merely follow after deluded thoughts.
Even that which is called "True Suchness" is devoid of any characteristics.

This refers to the ultimate limit of verbal expression, wherein words are dispelled by means of words; yet this essence of *tathatā* (suchness) has nothing that can be dispelled, because all phenomena are entirely *tathatā*.
Nor is there anything that can be established, because all phenomena are identical with *tathatā*.
One should know that because all phenomena are ineffable and inconceivable, they are called *tathatā* (suchness). Question:
"If this is the meaning, how can sentient beings accord with it and thereby gain entry?"
He replied:

"If one knows that although all phenomena are spoken of, there is neither a speaker nor anything to be spoken; and although they are contemplated, there is neither a contemplator nor anything to be contemplated—this is called 'conformity'."
"If one is free from discursive thought, it is called 'attaining entry.
Furthermore, regarding suchness (*tathatā*), there are two kinds of meanings based on verbal designations and conceptual discrimination.
What are these two?
First is emptiness as it truly is, because it can ultimately manifest reality.
Second is non-emptiness as it truly is, because it possesses its own essence and is fully endowed with the qualities of untainted nature.

That which is called "emptiness" refers to the fact that, from the very beginning, it has been dissociated from all defiled phenomena; that is to say, it is free from the differentiated characteristics of all dharmas because it is devoid of false mental conceptions.

One should know that the self-nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is neither characterized by existence, nor characterized by non-existence, nor characterized by neither existence nor non-existence; it is neither characterized by both existence and non-existence, nor characterized by unity, nor characterized by difference, nor characterized by neither unity nor difference, nor characterized by both unity and difference.

To state it in summary: based on all sentient beings, because their deluded minds engage in conceptual discrimination from moment to moment, these are said to be empty as they are all non-corresponding; yet if one is free from the deluded mind, there is truly nothing that can be called empty.

As for what is called "not empty": because the essence of phenomena has already been revealed as empty and devoid of falsehood, it is precisely the true mind—eternal, unchanging, and fully endowed with pure dharmas—and is therefore termed "not empty. Furthermore, there are no marks to be grasped, for this is a realm free from discursive thought that can only be realized through direct correspondence.

Regarding the arising and ceasing of the mind: based upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is the mind that arises and ceases; namely, the non-arising and non-ceasing [nature] and the arising and ceasing [phenomena] are conjoined, being neither identical nor different, and this is called the *ālayavijñāna*.
This consciousness has two meanings: it can encompass all phenomena and give rise to all phenomena.
What are these two? First, the meaning of awakening; second, the meaning of non-awakening.
What is called the meaning of "awakening" (bodhi) refers to the essence of mind being free from thought.

This state of being free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception; it is the single mark of the dharma-realm, which is the Tathāgata’s impartial dharmakāya. Based on this dharmakāya, it is designated as "original awakening" (mūlabodhi).

Why is this? The meaning of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-awakening*) is spoken in contrast to the meaning of initial enlightenment (*ādi-awakening*), because initial enlightenment is identical to original enlightenment.
As for the meaning of initial enlightenment, it exists because of original enlightenment, and it is said that there is initial enlightenment because of non-enlightenment (*a-awakening*).
Furthermore, because one awakens to the source of the mind, it is called ultimate awakening; because one does not awaken to the source of the mind, it is not ultimate awakening.
What is the meaning of this?

It is like an ordinary person who, perceiving that an evil thought has arisen in the preceding moment, is able to restrain the succeeding thought so that it does not arise; although this is called "awakening," it is in fact non-awakening.

The contemplative wisdom of the two vehicles and bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds perceive that thoughts are distinct; yet they realize that thoughts lack the characteristic of distinction. Because they have abandoned coarse conceptualizations and attachments, this is called "similar awakening.

Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body stage and those like them perceive the abiding of thoughts; yet they realize that thoughts lack the characteristic of abiding. Because they have departed from the characteristics of coarse conceptual thoughts, this is called "partial awakening.

When a bodhisattva reaches the end of the stages, fulfilling skillful means and attaining one-pointed correspondence with the mind, they realize that when the mind first arises, it has no characteristic of beginning. Because they are far removed from subtle thoughts, they see the nature of the mind, and the mind is then eternally abiding; this is called "ultimate awakening."
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"If there are sentient beings who can contemplate non-thought, they are thereby heading toward Buddha-wisdom.
Furthermore, as for the arising of the mind, there is no initial characteristic that can be known; yet to speak of knowing its initial characteristic is precisely what is meant by non-thought.

Therefore, all sentient beings are not called awakened; because from the very beginning their thoughts have continued in succession without ever being separated from discursive thought, they are said to possess beginningless ignorance.
If one attains non-thought, then one knows that the characteristics of the mind undergo arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.

Because of the equality of non-thought and so forth, there is in reality no distinction between initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*); for the four characteristics exist simultaneously and none possess independent self-existence, being fundamentally equal and identical to a single awakening.

Furthermore, when fundamental awakening (mūla-awakening) accords with defilement, it gives rise to two kinds of differentiated characteristics that are never separated from that fundamental awakening.
What are these two? First, the characteristic of the purity of wisdom; second, the characteristic of inconceivable activity.

Regarding the characteristic of the purity of wisdom: it refers to manifesting the Dharma-body through the purification of wisdom, by relying on the power of the熏習 (vāsanā) of the Dharma, practicing according to reality, and perfecting skillful means; thereby, one destroys the characteristics of the synthetic consciousness (*saṃghāta-vijñāna*) and extinguishes the characteristics of the continuous mind (*prabandha-citta*).
What is the meaning of this?
All characteristics of mind-consciousness are ignorance; yet the characteristic of ignorance does not depart from the nature of awakening, being neither destructible nor indestructible.

It is like the water of the great ocean, which surges with waves due to the wind; the characteristics of the water and the characteristics of the wind are not mutually separable, yet the water does not possess the nature of motion. If the wind ceases, the characteristic of motion is extinguished, but the moist nature remains undestroyed.

Thus, the intrinsically pure mind of sentient beings is stirred by the wind of ignorance; the mind and ignorance are both without form or characteristics and do not exist apart from one another, yet the mind is not of a nature that moves.
If ignorance ceases, the continuity of existence is extinguished, because the nature of wisdom is indestructible.

Regarding the characteristic of inconceivable activity: by relying on the purity of wisdom, it can produce all supreme and wondrous realms; that is to say, the characteristics of immeasurable merit are eternally uninterrupted, naturally corresponding to the faculties of sentient beings so that they may perceive them in various ways and thereby obtain benefit.
Furthermore, regarding the essential nature and characteristics of awakening, there are four kinds of great meanings that are equal to space, like a pure mirror.
What are these four?
The first is the mirror of emptiness as it truly is.
It is far removed from all marks of the objective realm of the mind, such that no dharma can appear, for this is not the meaning of cognitive illumination.
Second is the mirror of causal perfuming.

This refers to that which is truly non-empty, wherein all worldly realms appear; they neither emerge nor enter, neither perish nor decay, eternally abiding within the one mind because all dharmas are identical with true reality.
Furthermore, it cannot be defiled by any defiled phenomena, for the essence of wisdom is immovable and fully possesses the untainted [dharmas] that permeate sentient beings.
Third, it is the mirror of the transcendence of dharmas.

This refers to the non-empty dharma, which emerges from the hindrance of afflictions and the hindrance to knowledge, is free from the characteristics of composite phenomena, and is because it is purely clear and luminous.
Fourth is the mirror of the perfuming of conditions.

This means that because it issues forth from the Dharma and brings about liberation, it universally illumines the minds of sentient beings, causing them to cultivate roots of goodness by manifesting itself in accordance with their thoughts.

As for the meaning of "non-awakening," it refers to not knowing, as they truly are, that the Dharma of True Suchness is one; thus, non-awakening gives rise to the mind and its perceptions. These perceptions have no self-characteristic and are not separate from Original Awakening, just as a person who is lost becomes confused by relying on the directions, yet if they were to leave the directions behind, there would be no confusion.

Sentient beings are likewise: they are deluded by virtue of depending on awakening; yet if they were separated from the nature of awakening, there would be no non-awakening. Because they possess the deluded mind of non-awakening, they are able to understand names and meanings, and for their sake, true awakening is taught.
If one were apart from the mind of non-awakening, there would be no self-characteristic of true awakening that could be described.
Furthermore, based on non-awakening, three kinds of characteristics arise, which are associated with and inseparable from that non-awakening.
What are the three?
First is the phase of the karma of ignorance.
Because it relies on non-awakening, the mind moves; this is designated as "karma."
Awakening is non-movement;
movement entails suffering, because the fruit does not depart from its cause.
Second is the characteristic of being able to perceive.
Because it relies on movement, there is seeing;
without movement, there is no seeing.
Third is the characteristic of the objective realm.
Because one relies on the capacity for seeing, objects appear falsely;
apart from seeing, there are no objects.
Because there are conditions consisting of objects, six kinds of characteristics further arise.
What are the six? First is the characteristic of cognition (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*).
Based upon objects, the mind gives rise to discrimination between the pleasant and the unpleasant.
Second is the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*).
Because it relies upon cognition (*jñāna*), suffering and pleasure arise; for the mind awakens and thoughts arise in continuous correspondence without interruption.
Third is the characteristic of grasping (*udgraha-lakṣaṇa*).

First, the characteristic of the continuity of mental objects: because the mind gives rise to attachment while dwelling upon and maintaining experiences of suffering and pleasure by means of continuous recollection of objects.

Second, the characteristic of the appearance of objects: because one discriminates the appearances of provisional names and words based on false attachments. Third, the characteristic of the appearance of birth and death: because one discriminates the appearances of the body and its environment based on the continuity of the seeds of karma and afflictions. Fourth, the characteristic of the appearance of names: because one discriminates the appearances of provisional names and words based on deluded clinging.
Fifth is the characteristic of initiating karma.
Because one relies on names and designations, seeking them out and grasping at them, one creates various kinds of karma.
Sixth is the characteristic of suffering bound by karma.
Because one lacks mastery over the retribution received due to dependence on karma,
one should know that ignorance can give rise to all defiled phenomena, for all defiled phenomena are characterized by non-awakening.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of characteristics regarding awakening and non-awakening. What are these two?
First, the characteristic of similarity; second, the characteristic of difference.

Regarding their identical characteristics: for example, various earthenware vessels all share the same nature and characteristics as fine dust; likewise, the various karmic illusions of both outflow-free states and ignorance all share the same nature and characteristics as True Suchness (tathatā).

Therefore, based on this meaning of *tathatā* (suchness), the *Sūtras* state that all sentient beings have been primordially and eternally abiding in *nirvāṇa*. The dharma of *bodhi* is neither a characteristic to be cultivated nor a characteristic to be produced; it is ultimately unattainable and possesses no visible form or appearance.

As for those who perceive such forms and appearances, these are merely the products of illusory activity following along with defilement; they are not the nature of non-empty wisdom-form, because the characteristics of wisdom are invisible.

Regarding "different characteristics": just as various earthenware vessels are each distinct from one another, so too are the distinctions between the illusions of outflow-free ignorance and the illusions of defiled ignorance, due to the differences in their respective natures of defilement and illusion.
Furthermore, regarding the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing: it is because sentient beings revolve in dependence upon mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
What is the meaning of this?

It is because, based on the *ālaya-vijñāna*, there arises ignorance and non-awakening; it is able to see, to manifest, and to grasp objects, giving rise to a continuous succession of thoughts; therefore, it is called "thought" (*manas*).
This mind has five further names. What are these five?
First, it is called the "karmic consciousness" (*karma-vijñāna*), meaning that by the power of ignorance, the mind moves without awareness.
Second is called the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), so named because it relies on the moving mind and is able to perceive objects.
Third is called the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*), which is able to manifest all objective realms, just as a clear mirror manifests forms and images;

the manifesting consciousness is likewise, for as each of the five sense-objects arrives in opposition, it manifests them immediately without sequence, arising spontaneously at all times and always remaining present.
Fourth is called the *jñāna-vijñāna* (cognition of wisdom), which refers to the discrimination between defiled and pure phenomena.

Fifth is called the *saṃtati-vijñāna* (continuity consciousness), because it is associated with mindfulness that is uninterrupted; it maintains the karmic actions—both good and evil—of immeasurable past lives so that they are not lost, and it can bring to fruition the retributions of suffering and pleasure in the present and future without error. Furthermore, it causes one to suddenly recall events already experienced in the present, and to unconsciously harbor deluded anxieties regarding future matters.
Therefore, the three realms are illusory and are produced solely by the mind; apart from the mind, there are no objects of the six sense-fields.
What is the meaning of this?

It is because all phenomena arise from the mind through the production of deluded thoughts; all discrimination is simply the discrimination of one's own mind, and when the mind does not perceive the mind, no characteristics can be apprehended.

One should know that all worldly objects of experience exist and are sustained solely by the ignorant, deluded mind of sentient beings; therefore, all phenomena are like reflections in a mirror, having no substantial essence to be found, being nothing but the false constructions of the mind.
This is because when the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease.

Furthermore, that which is called the "mental consciousness" (manovijñāna) is this very continuous consciousness (*saṃtati-vijñāna*). It is so named because it relies on the deep-seated attachments of ordinary beings who calculate in terms of "self" and "what belongs to self," following various deluded grasps as they攀缘 (cling to) objects according to circumstances. Its differentiation of the six sense-objects is termed the mental consciousness, and it is also called the "separating consciousness" (*prativijñapti-vijñāna*).
Furthermore, it is also called the "discriminative consciousness of phenomena" (*vastu-vijñapti-vijñāna*), because this consciousness increases based on the afflictions of views and craving.
As for the consciousness that arises through the permeation of ignorance, it cannot be known by ordinary beings, nor can it be realized by the wisdom of the two vehicles.

This means that based on a bodhisattva who, from the initial stage of right faith, gives rise to the mind of enlightenment and engages in contemplation, even if they realize the dharma-body and attain some partial knowledge, they cannot know it exhaustively until reaching the ultimate stage of a bodhisattva; only a Buddha fully comprehends it.
Why is this? This mind has been intrinsically pure from the very beginning, yet it possesses ignorance; being defiled by ignorance, there arises a defiled mind.
Although it possesses a defiled mind, it is eternally constant and unchanging; therefore, this meaning can be known only by a Buddha.

That which is called the nature of the mind is termed "unchanging" because it is eternally free from thought. Because one does not realize the single Dharma-realm, the mind becomes dissociated [from its true nature], and the sudden arising of thought is termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
There are six kinds of defiled minds. What are the six?
First is the defilement associated with grasping, which is removed through the liberation of the two vehicles and by relying on the stage of faith.

Second is the defilement associated with non-interruption (*anuccheda-saṃprayukta-kleśa*), which is gradually abandoned through the practice of skillful means based on the stage of faith-correspondence (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), because one attains ultimate separation upon reaching the stage of pure mind (*śuddha-citta-bhūmi*).

Third, the defilement associated with the discrimination of knowledge (*vikalpa-jñāna-saṃprayukta-kleśa*), which is gradually abandoned from the stage of possessing the precepts (*śīla-bhūmi*) until it is ultimately abandoned at the stage of the skillful means of signlessness (*animitta-upāya-bhūmi*).
Fourth, the defilement dissociated from manifested form (*rūpa-viprayukta-kleśa*), which can be abandoned by relying on the stage of mastery over form (*rūpa-vaśitā-bhūmi*).
Fifth, one is able to see the defilements dissociated from the mind, for these can be abandoned by relying on the stage of mastery over the mind (*svabhūmi*).

Sixth, one is able to abandon the fundamental karmic defilements dissociated from the mind, for these can be abandoned by entering the stage of the Tathāgata through the Bodhisattva’s stage of completion (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*).

Those who do not understand the meaning of the single dharma-realm observe and train in its severance from the stage of "conformity with faith," attain detachment according to their capacity upon entering the "pure mind" stage, and finally achieve ultimate detachment at the stage of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the meaning of "conformity" (saṃprayoga): it refers to the fact that while the mind, mental factors, and dharmas are distinct, they are known to share the same characteristics of cognition and objects based on the differentiation between defilement and purity.

Regarding the meaning of "non-conformity" (asaṃprayoga): it refers to the fact that the mind itself is non-awakened and eternally lacks differentiation, and thus does not possess the same characteristics of cognition and objects as [the mental factors].
Furthermore, the meaning of "defiled mind" is termed the "obstruction of afflictions," because it can obstruct the fundamental wisdom of *tathatā*.
The meaning of "ignorance" is termed the "obstruction of wisdom," because it can obstruct the spontaneous wisdom of mundane activity.
What is the meaning of this?
It is because, by relying on the defiled mind, one is able to see, manifest, and falsely grasp at objects, thereby contravening the nature of equality.
This is because all phenomena are eternally quiescent and devoid of the characteristic of arising, yet through the non-awakening of ignorance, one falsely opposes these phenomena.
Because they are unable to attain the various kinds of knowledge that accord with all worldly objects.
Furthermore, there are two types of those who conceptualize the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
What are these two?
First is the coarse, because it is associated with the mind;
second is the subtle, because it is dissociated from the mind.
Furthermore, that which is coarse among the coarse is the realm of ordinary beings;
that which is subtle among the coarse and coarse among the subtle is the realm of bodhisattvas;
and that which is subtle among the subtle is the realm of the Buddhas.
These two kinds of arising and ceasing exist based on the perfuming of ignorance; that is to say, they depend upon causes and they depend upon conditions.
Dependence upon causes refers to the meaning of non-awakening;
dependence upon conditions refers to the meaning of the deluded construction of objective realms.
If the cause ceases, then the condition ceases; because the cause ceases, the dissociated mind ceases, and because the condition ceases, the associated mind ceases.
Question:
"If the mind ceases, how does it continue in succession?"
"If there is continuity, why do you say there is ultimate cessation? He replied:
"What is called 'cessation' refers only to the cessation of the mind's manifestations, not the cessation of the essence of the mind."
Just as wind possesses the characteristic of movement by depending upon water, if the water were to cease, the characteristic of wind would be severed and have no basis for subsistence.
Because the water does not cease, the characteristic of wind continues; it is only when the wind ceases that the characteristic of movement follows in cessation, not because the water has ceased.
Ignorance is likewise; it moves in dependence upon the substance of the mind. If the substance of the mind were to perish, sentient beings would be severed and have nothing to rely upon.

Because the substance does not perish, the mind can continue in succession. It is only because delusion perishes that the characteristics of the mind perish along with it, but the wisdom of the mind does not perish.
Furthermore, because there is the principle of the perfuming of four kinds of dharmas, defiled and pure dharmas arise without interruption.
What are these four?
First, the pure dharma is called *tathatā* (suchness).
Second, all causes of defilement are called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Third, the deluded mind is called the karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).
Fourth, deluded objects—namely, the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*)—are so named.
Regarding the meaning of perfuming (*vāsanā*): it is like a worldly garment that originally has no fragrance; yet, because a person perfumes it with incense, it comes to possess a fragrant scent.

This is likewise the case here: although the pure dharma of *tathatā* (suchness) is fundamentally free from defilement, because it is perfumed by ignorance (*avidyā*), the appearance of defilement arises.
In the defiled dharmas of ignorance, there is truly no pure karma; however, because they are perfumed by True Suchness (tathatā), they possess the function of purity.
How is it that this perfuming gives rise to the uninterrupted continuity of defiled dharmas?
That is to say: because there is ignorance based upon the dharma of true suchness (tathatā), the defiled dharmas of ignorance act as a cause to permeate (vāsanā) true suchness;
because of this permeation, there arises the deluded mind (vikalpa-citta), and because of the existence of the deluded mind, it in turn permeates ignorance.
Because they do not understand the dharma of suchness, they fail to realize that thoughts arise and manifest as delusive objects.

Due to these delusive objects acting as conditions for defiled dharmas, they in turn perfuse the deluded mind, causing it to become attached through its thoughts and to create various karmas, thereby undergoing all manner of suffering of body and mind.
The meaning of the perfuming of these false objects is twofold. What are the two?
First, the perfuming that increases the proliferation of thought; second, the perfuming that increases grasping.
The meaning of the perfuming of the deluded mind is twofold. What are these two?
First is the fundamental perfuming of the karma-consciousness, which enables arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and all bodhisattvas to undergo the suffering of birth and death.

Second, it increases the habitual tendencies of the *vikaḷpa-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of objects), whereby one is able to undergo the suffering bound by the karma of ordinary beings.
There are two kinds of meanings regarding the habitual tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā*).
What are these two?
First is the fundamental perfuming, because it has the sense of being able to accomplish the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*).
Second is the perfuming of views and attachments that arise from it, because it has the sense of being able to accomplish the discerning consciousness of phenomena (*vikalpa-vastu-vijñāna*).
How does the perfuming that gives rise to pure dharmas proceed without interruption?

It is because the True Suchness (tathatā) exists that it can perfume ignorance; by the power of these perfuming causes and conditions, it causes the deluded mind to grow weary of the suffering of birth and death and to joyfully seek nirvana.
Because this deluded mind possesses the causes and conditions of aversion and seeking, it immediately perfumes the *tathatā* (suchness).

Confident in its own nature, it realizes that the mind is falsely moving and that no external objects exist; thus, it cultivates the dharma of detachment. Because it knows with suchness that no external objects exist, it gives rise to various skillful means and practices in accordance with reality—neither grasping nor conceptualizing. Eventually, through the power of long-term perfuming, ignorance is extinguished.

Because ignorance ceases, the mind does not arise; because it does not arise, its objects likewise cease; because both causes and conditions have ceased, the characteristics of the mind are entirely exhausted—this is called attaining nirvana and accomplishing spontaneous karma.
The meaning of the perfuming of the deluded mind is twofold. What are these two?

First is the perfuming of the *vikalpa-vastu-vijñāna* (the consciousness that discriminates phenomena), which pertains to ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles who, weary of the suffering of birth and death, gradually advance toward the Unsurpassed Way according to their respective capacities.
Second is the熏習 (xūnxí, perfuming) of the mind, which refers to the fact that bodhisattvas, having generated a courageous resolve, swiftly proceed toward nirvana.
There are two types of meaning regarding the perfuming of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
What are these two? First is the perfuming of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-vāsanā*), and second is the perfuming of activity (*vṛtti-vāsanā*).

As for the perfuming of the intrinsic nature: from beginningless time, it is endowed with the complete possession of untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) and possesses the nature of performing inconceivable karma as the objective sphere.

Constantly perfumed by these two meanings, and because they possess power, they enable sentient beings to become weary of the suffering of birth and death, to joyfully seek nirvana, to have confidence that their own bodies possess the *tathatā* dharma, and to resolve to practice.
Question:

"If this is the meaning, then since all sentient beings possess *tathatā* (suchness) equally and are all subject to perfuming (*vāsanā*), why are there immeasurable distinctions between those who have faith and those who lack it, as well as differences in their temporal sequence?"
"All should simultaneously realize for themselves that they possess the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma and diligently cultivate skillful means to enter *nirvāṇa*.
He replied:

"Although *tathatā* is fundamentally one, there are immeasurable and boundless instances of ignorance (*avidyā*). From the very beginning, their intrinsic natures have differed in degree—some being thick and others thin."

The distinctions among the higher afflictions (*kleśa*) that exceed the sands of the Ganges arise based on ignorance; likewise, the distinctions among the afflictions of self-view, craving, and attachment arise based on ignorance.
Because all such afflictions arise depending upon ignorance and possess immeasurable distinctions throughout their preceding and succeeding stages, only the Tathāgata is able to know them.
Furthermore, all Buddha-dharmas have causes and conditions; they are accomplished only when causes and conditions are fully present.
For example, although the nature of fire within wood is the direct cause of fire, it is impossible for it to burn the wood by itself without someone knowing of it and employing skillful means.

Sentient beings are likewise; although they possess the power of the perfuming of the direct cause, if they do not encounter Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, spiritual friends, and others to serve as conditions, it is impossible for them to spontaneously sever their afflictions and enter nirvana.

Even if there is the power of external conditions, if the internal pure dharmas have not yet acquired the power of perfuming, one will still be unable to ultimately weary of the suffering of saṃsāra or joyfully seek nirvāṇa.

If the causes and conditions are fully present—namely, possessing the power of one's own habitual perfuming, and being protected by the compassionate vows of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—one is able to give rise to a mind that loathes suffering, believe in the existence of nirvana, and cultivate roots of goodness.

Because the roots of goodness have been cultivated to maturity, one encounters Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who provide instruction, benefit, and joy; thus, one is able to advance toward and enter the path to Nirvana.
That which functions through perfuming is the power of external conditions for sentient beings.
Thus, external conditions have immeasurable meanings, which are briefly explained as two kinds.
What are these two? First, differentiated conditions; second, equal conditions.

Regarding the specific condition (*viśeṣa-pratyaya*): this person relies upon the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others, from the initial generation of the aspiration for enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood. Throughout this interval, whether they are seen or remembered—whether as kinsmen, parents, or relatives; as servants; as friends; or as enemies; or through the practice of the four means of attraction (*saṃgraha-vastu*)—all such immeasurable activities and conditions serve to give rise to the power of the habitual perfuming of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). This enables sentient beings to increase their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), because they obtain benefit through seeing or hearing [the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas].
These conditions are of two kinds. What are the two?
First, proximate conditions, because one attains liberation swiftly.
Second is the distant condition, because they attain deliverance after a long period of time.
These two conditions—the proximate and the distant—are further divided into two types each. What are these two?
First is the condition for increasing practice; second is the condition for receiving the Way.
As for the condition of equality, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas universally vow to deliver all sentient beings, naturally perfuming them through constant and uninterrupted cultivation.
By virtue of the power of the wisdom of identical essence, he manifests activities according to what is seen and heard as appropriate.
This is because sentient beings, by relying upon samādhi, are able to see all Buddhas with equanimity.
This cultivation of essence and function is further divided into two types.
What are these two?

First is that which is not yet in accord [with non-conceptual wisdom], referring to ordinary beings, followers of the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas who have newly resolved to attain enlightenment; they cultivate through the熏習 (perfuming) of the manas and the mental consciousness, and are able to practice by relying on the power of faith.
First, because they have not yet attained a non-conceptual mind that accords with its essence, nor have they attained mastery over karma and practice that accords with its function.

Second, they have already attained such accord: this refers to Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body who have attained the non-conceptual mind and accord with the wisdom and functions of all Buddhas; relying solely on the power of the Dharma, they naturally engage in practice, perfuming True Suchness and thereby extinguishing ignorance.
Furthermore, the perfuming of defiled dharmas has continued uninterrupted from time immemorial, ceasing only upon the attainment of Buddhahood;
the perfuming of pure dharmas, however, is never interrupted and persists until the end of the future.
What is the meaning of this?

Because the dharma of True Suchness (tathatā) constantly perfumes [the mind], the deluded mind is extinguished and the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) manifests; since it gives rise to the perfuming of its functional activity, there is no interruption.

Furthermore, as for the essential nature and characteristics of True Suchness (Tathatā): it neither increases nor decreases among all ordinary beings, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Buddhas; it is not born in the past limit (pūrvānta) and does not perish in the future limit (aparānta), being ultimately eternal and constant.
From the very beginning, its nature has been spontaneously replete with all merits.

This is because it possesses the meaning of the great light of intrinsic wisdom; the meaning of universally illuminating the Dharma-realm; the meaning of true and authentic cognition; the meaning of the intrinsically pure mind; the meaning of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; and the meaning of coolness, immutability, and sovereignty.

Because it is fully endowed with such Buddha-dharmas—more numerous than the sands of the Ganges—which are inseparable, uninterrupted, non-different, and inconceivable, and because it is perfected to the point that not even the slightest meaning is lacking, it is called the Tathāgatagarbha and is also called the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.
Question: "It was stated above that the essence of True Suchness (tathatā) is equal and free from all marks; why, then, is it further said that its essence possesses such various kinds of merit?"
He replied:
"Although these various meanings of merit do indeed exist, they possess no marks of distinction; they are equal in a single flavor, being nothing other than True Suchness alone."
What is the meaning of this?
Because it is non-conceptual and free from the marks of conceptualization,
it is therefore non-dual.
Furthermore, by what principle can these distinctions be explained?
They are shown through the characteristics of arising and ceasing based upon the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*). How are they shown?

Because all phenomena are fundamentally mind-only and truly devoid of thought, yet there exists a deluded mind; because it fails to awaken and gives rise to thoughts, perceiving various objective realms, it is called ignorance.
The non-arising of the mind-nature is precisely the meaning of the radiance of great wisdom.
If the mind gives rise to views, there will be the characteristic of non-seeing.
When the mind-nature is free from views, it is precisely the meaning of universally illuminating the Dharma-realm.

If the mind is subject to movement, it is not true cognition; it lacks intrinsic nature and is neither permanent, nor blissful, nor self, nor pure. It is characterized by feverish affliction and decay, thus lacking sovereignty, and even possesses meanings of deluded defilement exceeding those of the sands of the Ganges.
Regarding this meaning, when the nature of the mind is unmoving, there is the manifestation of the characteristics of all pure merits, numbering more than the sands of the Ganges.
If the mind gives rise to activity and perceives further phenomena as objects of recollection, then there is deficiency.
Such immeasurable merits of the pure dharmas are themselves the one mind, with nothing further to be contemplated; therefore, they are fulfilled.
This is called the Tathāgata-garbha of the Dharma-body.

Furthermore, as for the function of True Suchness (tathatā), it refers to the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, who originally, while on the ground of practice (bhūmi), gave rise to great compassion, cultivated the various pāramitās, and gathered and transformed sentient beings.
They establish great vows, desiring to deliver all beings within the realm of sentient beings without exception.

They do not limit themselves by the number of kalpas, extending until the end of the future; for they regard all sentient beings as their own self, yet they do not grasp at the mark of a sentient being.
What is the meaning of this?
It means that one knows, as it truly is, that all sentient beings and one’s own body are equal in *tathatā* (suchness) and without distinction.

Because one possesses such great wisdom of skillful means, ignorance is extinguished and the fundamental *dharmakāya* is seen. Thereupon, inconceivable karmic activities of various kinds arise spontaneously; these are equal to *tathatā* and pervade all places, yet no marks of activity can be apprehended therein.

Why is this? It is because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are solely the body of the marks of Dharma-body wisdom; in the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), there are no realms of conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). They are free from purposeful activity, yet they are said to possess "function" only because sentient beings gain benefit through seeing and hearing them.
This function is of two kinds. What are the two?

First, that which is perceived by the minds of ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles, based on the *vibhava-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of phenomena), is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).

Because they do not know that the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are manifesting, they perceive [the Buddha] as coming from outside; because they grasp at the boundaries of form (*rūpa*), they are unable to know it exhaustively.

Second, based on the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*): this refers to what is perceived by the minds of all Bodhisattvas, from their first aspiration (*prathama-cittotpāda*) up to the ultimate stage of a Bodhisattva; this is called the Reward Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*).

The body possesses immeasurable colors; these colors possess immeasurable marks; these marks possess immeasurable secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). Furthermore, the various adornments of the supporting fruits upon which it rests are also immeasurable and diverse, manifesting according to what is shown. Thus, they are boundless and inexhaustible, free from the characteristic of limitation; as appropriate to each case, they can constantly be maintained, neither destroyed nor lost.

Such merits are all accomplished through the permeation of the untainted practices of the various pāramitās and the inconceivable permeation; because they are fully endowed with immeasurable marks of bliss, they are called the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya).

Furthermore, that which is perceived by ordinary beings is its coarse form; as it is seen differently according to each of the six realms of existence, consisting of various distinct categories that do not possess the characteristics of experiencing bliss, it is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (Emanation Body).

Furthermore, as for what is seen by bodhisattvas who have first resolved upon enlightenment: because they have deep faith in the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness), they see it only partially; yet they know that matters such as the adornment of those physical forms are without coming or going, free from spatial limitations, appearing solely in dependence upon the mind, and not separate from *tathatā*.
Nevertheless, this bodhisattva still engages in conceptual discrimination because they have not yet entered the stage of the dharmakāya.

Once they attain the pure mind, what they perceive becomes subtle and its function becomes increasingly superior, until, reaching the end of the bodhisattva stages, their vision reaches its ultimate consummation.

If one is separated from the *karmic consciousness*, there is no appearance of seeing, because the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas possesses no such color-forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) that could be seen by one another.
Question:
"If the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is devoid of color-forms, how is it able to manifest color-forms?"
He replied:
"Because this very Dharma-body is the substance of form, it is able to manifest as form.
That is to say, from the very beginning, form and mind have been non-dual; since the nature of form is itself wisdom, the substance of form has no shape, and is therefore called the Wisdom-body."
Because the nature of wisdom is itself form, it is said that the Dharma-body pervades all places.

The forms manifested therein have no boundaries; according to the mind, they can manifest throughout the worlds of the ten directions, with immeasurable bodhisattvas, immeasurable reward-bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*), and immeasurable adornments, each distinct from the others. Yet, all are without boundaries and do not obstruct one another.
"This cannot be known through the conceptual discrimination of mind-consciousness, because it is the meaning of the sovereign function of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, this demonstrates the entry from the gate of arising and ceasing directly into the gate of True Suchness.

That is to say, when one investigates the five aggregates—the relationship between form and mind—and the objects of the six sense-fields, they are ultimately devoid of thought. Because the mind has no form or appearance, even if one searches for it throughout the ten directions, it can never be found.
Just as a person, due to delusion, might take east for west while the directions themselves do not actually shift, so it is with sentient beings:
because of the delusion of ignorance, they take the mind to be thought, though the mind itself is truly unmoving.
If one can observe and know that the mind is without thought, one immediately attains compliance with and entry into the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Regarding the counteracting of false attachments: all false attachments depend upon the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*); if one is free from the self, there will be no false attachments.
This view of self is of two kinds. What are the two?
First, the view of a self in persons; second, the view of a self in phenomena.
Regarding the view of self and others, it is said that there are five types based on the teachings for ordinary worldlings. What are these five?

First, having heard the sūtras state that the Tathāgata’s dharma-body is ultimately quiescent and like empty space, because they do not understand that this was taught to destroy attachment, they claim that empty space itself is the nature of the Tathāgata.
How is this countered?
It is clarified that the characteristic of space is a false dharma; its essence is unreal. It exists only in contrast to form; as a visible characteristic, it causes the mind to arise and perish.
Since all phenomena of form are fundamentally the mind, there is in reality no external form.
If there were no form, then even the characteristics of empty space would not exist.

What is called "all objective realms" exists only because the mind falsely arises; if the mind is free from false movement, then all objective realms cease, and there remains only the single true mind, which is omnipresent.
This refers to the ultimate meaning of the Tathāgata’s vast nature and wisdom, for it is not like the characteristics of empty space.

Second, one hears the sūtras teaching that all worldly phenomena are ultimately empty in essence, and even the dharmas of nirvāṇa and *tathatā* (suchness) are ultimately empty; from the very beginning they have been empty by nature, free from all marks.
Because they do not understand that [the teaching on emptiness] is intended to destroy attachment, they claim that the nature of *tathatā* and *nirvāṇa* is merely empty.
How is this to be remedied?
It is clarified that the self-substance of the *dharmakāya* of *tathatā* is not empty, for it is fully endowed with immeasurable intrinsic merits.
Third, when they hear the sūtras state that the Tathāgata-garbha neither increases nor decreases and that its essence is fully endowed with all dharmas of merit,
because they do not understand this, they claim that the Tathāgata-garbha possesses the distinct characteristics of material and mental phenomena.
How is this countered?

Because it is taught solely by relying on the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness), whereas the distinctions [of phenomena] are manifested and taught based on the meaning of the defiled nature of arising and ceasing.

Fourth, when one hears the *sūtras* state that all worldly phenomena of birth and death and all defiled dharmas exist in dependence upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, and that all dharmas do not depart from *tathatā*.
Because of this lack of understanding, it is claimed that the *tathāgatagarbha* inherently possesses all the phenomena of worldly birth and death.
How is this countered?

It is because the *tathāgatagarbha* has, from the very beginning, possessed only pure merits exceeding the sands of the Ganges, which are inseparable from, uninterrupted by, and non-different from the meaning of *tathatā*.

Because the defiled dharmas of afflictions, which exceed the sands of the Ganges in number, are merely illusory existences whose nature is inherently non-existent from the beginning; since time immemorial, they have never been associated with the Tathāgatagarbha.
If the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha inherently possessed deluded phenomena, such that its realization would cause those delusions to cease forever, this would be impossible.
Fifth, one hears the Sūtras state that because of the Tathāgatagarbha there is saṃsāra, and because of the Tathāgatagarbha one attains nirvāṇa.
Because they do not understand this, they claim that sentient beings have a beginning.
Because they perceive such a beginning, they further claim that the nirvāṇa attained by the Tathāgata has an end, and that he returns once more to become a sentient being.
How is this countered?
Because the Tathāgatagarbha has no prior limit, the characteristics of ignorance likewise have no beginning.
If one were to say that there are sentient beings who first arise outside the triple world, that would be a teaching from the scriptures of the non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, the Tathāgatagarbha has no posterior limit; because the nirvāṇa attained by all Buddhas is in accord with it, it likewise has no posterior limit.

As for those who hold the view of a self in phenomena (dharma-ātman), because they possess the dull faculties of the two vehicles, the Tathāgata teaches them only the non-self of the person (pudgala-nairātmya).
Because the teaching is not ultimate, they perceive the five aggregates as phenomena subject to arising and ceasing; thus, they fear birth and death and falsely grasp at nirvana.
How is this to be remedied?
Because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) do not arise by way of their own nature (*svabhāva*), they do not cease; they are *nirvāṇa* from the very beginning.

Furthermore, for one who has ultimately abandoned false attachments, it should be known that defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*) and pure phenomena (*vyavadāna-dharma*) are entirely mutually dependent and possess no self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that can be described. Therefore, all phenomena have, from the very outset, been neither form nor mind, neither wisdom (*jñāna*) nor consciousness (*vijñāna*), neither existent nor non-existent; they are ultimately inexpressible in their characteristics.

As for the existence of verbal expressions, you should know that these are the Tathāgata’s skillful means, employing provisional speech to guide sentient beings. Their ultimate intent is entirely to lead them away from discursive thought and back to True Suchness (*tathatā*), because contemplating all dharmas causes the mind to undergo arising and ceasing, thereby preventing entry into true wisdom.

Regarding the characteristics of the various ways of setting out upon the path: this refers to the path realized by all Buddhas, in the sense that all Bodhisattvas set their minds on awakening, practice, and proceed toward it.
Briefly stated, there are three kinds of generating the mind [of enlightenment].
What are these three?

First, the generation of the mind through the perfection of faith; second, the generation of the mind through practice based on understanding; and third, the generation of the mind through realization.

Regarding the arousal of the mind through the perfection of faith: based on what kind of person and by practicing what kind of conduct does one attain the perfection of faith and become capable of arousing the mind?

It is said that based on sentient beings of the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*), because they possess the power of cultivated roots of goodness, they believe in the retribution of karma and are able to give rise to the ten wholesome actions. They come to loathe the suffering of birth and death and desire to seek unsurpassed bodhi. Having encountered various Buddhas, they personally attend to, make offerings to, and practice with confidence. Because their confidence is perfected after ten thousand *kalpas*, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas instruct them to arouse the mind;
or, out of great compassion, they are able to arouse the mind themselves.
Or, because the True Dharma is about to perish, one may spontaneously resolve to awaken for the sake of protecting the Dharma.

Those who achieve such faith and thus give rise to the resolve enter the stage of the right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), from which they never again regress; this is called abiding in the lineage of the Tathāgata, in accordance with the primary cause.

If there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness are meager and whose afflictions have been deep and heavy for a long time, even though they encounter a Buddha and are able to make offerings, they will nevertheless plant the seeds for rebirth as humans or devas, or plant the seeds for the two vehicles.
Suppose there are those who seek the Mahāyāna, whose faculties are not fixed and who may advance or retreat.

Some may have made offerings to various Buddhas for less than ten thousand kalpas, yet within that time, encountering the right conditions, they may likewise resolve their minds upon enlightenment—namely, by perceiving the physical marks of a Buddha and thereby generating the aspiration;
or by making offerings to the Saṃgha and thereby generating the aspiration.
Or they may be taught by followers of the Two Vehicles to resolve their minds [for enlightenment], or they may learn to resolve their minds by following others.
Such resolutions of mind are entirely uncertain; encountering adverse conditions, they may suddenly fall back and descend to the stage of the Two Vehicles.
Furthermore, regarding those who have resolved their minds through the perfection of faith: what kind of mind do they resolve upon?
Briefly stated, there are three types.
What are these three?
First is the straightforward mind, because it maintains right mindfulness of the dharma of True Suchness.
Second is the profound mind, because it delights in accumulating all virtuous practices.
Third is the mind of great compassion, because it desires to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings.
Question:

"It was stated above that the Dharma-realm has a single characteristic and the essence of the Buddha is non-dual; for what reason, then, do you not simply contemplate True Suchness alone, but instead rely on seeking and practicing all manner of wholesome deeds?"
He replied:
"It is like a great maṇi jewel whose essential nature is luminous and pure, yet which is defiled by the impurities of ore.
Even if a person contemplates its precious nature, if they do not employ various skillful means to grind and polish it, it will never attain purity."
In this way, although the dharma-body of the true suchness (tathatā) of sentient beings is empty and pure by nature, it is nevertheless defiled by immeasurable afflictions.
Even if a person contemplates true suchness, they will not attain purity unless they cultivate it through various skillful means (upāya).
Because defilements are immeasurable and pervade all phenomena, one cultivates all wholesome practices as their antidote.
If a person practices all wholesome dharmas, they will naturally accord with and conform to the Dharma of True Suchness (tathatā).
Briefly stated, there are four kinds of skillful means (*upāya*). What are the four?
First, the skillful means of practicing the root.
This means that one contemplates how the self-nature of all phenomena is unborn and, being free from false views, does not abide in birth and death.

One contemplates how all phenomena arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions and that the fruits of karma are never lost; thus, giving rise to great compassion, one cultivates various merits to gather and transform sentient beings, yet does not abide in nirvana, because one accords with the non-abiding nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Second is the skillful means of cessation.
This refers to shame, remorse, and repentance, which can halt all unwholesome dharmas from increasing, because by conforming to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one becomes free from all faults.
Third is the skillful means for initiating and increasing roots of goodness.

This refers to diligently making offerings to and prostrating before the Triple Gem; praising, rejoicing in, and entreating all Buddhas. Because of a heart of pure devotion and reverence toward the Triple Gem, one’s faith increases, whereby one is able to aspire to seek the unsurpassed Way.

Furthermore, because they are protected by the power of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, they are able to eliminate karmic obstacles and their roots of goodness do not regress, as they accord with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) and are free from the obstacle of delusion.
Fourth is the skillful means of the equality of great vows.

This refers to making the vow to continue until the end of the future, transforming and delivering all sentient beings without exception, causing them all to ultimately attain *nirvāṇa* without remainder. Because this accords with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) without interruption—the nature of phenomena being vast, pervading all sentient beings, equal and non-dual, free from thoughts of self and other, and ultimately quiescent—[this vow is established].
Because the bodhisattva has given rise to this mind, they obtain a partial vision of the dharmakāya.
By virtue of seeing the dharmakāya, they are able to manifest eight kinds of benefits for sentient beings according to their power of aspiration.

That is to say: descending from Tuṣita Heaven, entering the womb, dwelling in the womb, emerging from the womb, leaving the household life, attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering parinirvāṇa.

However, this bodhisattva is not yet called "Dharmakāya," because the tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*) accumulated over immeasurable past eons has not been definitively severed; thus, in whatever place they are born, they remain associated with subtle suffering. Yet, they are not bound by karma, owing to the power of their sovereign great vows.

As stated in the sūtras, although it is said that some may fall back and descend into the evil realms, this is not an actual falling back; rather, it is spoken for the sake of inspiring those beginner bodhisattvas who have not yet entered the stage of certainty and who are prone to indolence, so as to cause them to become courageous and diligent.
Furthermore, once this bodhisattva has awakened the mind, he remains far removed from timidity and ultimately never fears falling into the stages of the two vehicles.

Even if he hears that it takes immeasurable, boundless, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of diligent toil and difficult practices to attain *nirvāṇa*, he does not become timid, because through faith he knows that all phenomena have been *nirvāṇa* from the very beginning.
It should be known that the generation of the mind through the stage of practice and understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) is even more excellent.

This is because, from the time of initial right faith until the first *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* is nearly completed, this bodhisattva has attained a profound understanding that manifests within the dharma of *tathatā*, and their cultivation is free from signs (*animitta*).
Because one knows that the essence of the dharma-nature is devoid of stinginess and greed, one practices the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) in accordance with it;
because one knows that the dharma-nature is undefiled and free from the faults of the five desires, one practices the perfection of ethical discipline (śīla-pāramitā) in accordance with it;
because one knows that the dharma-nature is without suffering and free from anger and affliction, one practices the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) in accordance with it.

Because they know that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is devoid of the characteristics of body and mind, and are thus free from indolence, they practice the perfection of vigor (vīrya-pāramitā) in accordance with it;
because they know that the nature of phenomena is eternally concentrated, its essence being without distraction, they practice the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā) in accordance with it;
because they know that the essence of the nature of phenomena is luminous, being free from ignorance (avidyā), they practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā) in accordance with it.

Regarding the realization of the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*), from the Stage of Pure Mind (*śuddhacittabhūmi*) up to the Ultimate Stage of the Bodhisattva (*niṣṭhāgatabodhisattvabhūmi*), what realm is realized?

It is called *tathatā* (suchness); it is designated as a "realm" based on the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*). However, for this realization, there is no objective realm; only the wisdom of *tathatā* is termed the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

In a single moment of thought, this bodhisattva is able to reach all worlds throughout the ten directions without exception, making offerings to all Buddhas and requesting them to turn the wheel of Dharma, solely for the purpose of guiding, benefiting, and bringing happiness to sentient beings.
One does not rely on the literal letter; for the sake of those sentient beings who are timid, one may manifest the transcendence of stages and the swift attainment of perfect enlightenment;
or, for the sake of those sentient beings who are indolent, one may say, "I shall attain the Buddha-way after immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas."

He is able to demonstrate such countless, inconceivable skillful means; yet in reality, the bodhisattvas' spiritual lineages and faculties are equal, their resolve is equal, and what they realize is also equal, with no dharma by which one may surpass another.

Because all bodhisattvas pass through three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, it is only due to the differences among the worlds of sentient beings—wherein what is seen, heard, and the faculties, desires, and natures vary—that the practices they manifest also appear to have distinctions.
Furthermore, regarding the characteristics of a bodhisattva’s arousal of the mind, there are three subtle aspects of the mind.
What are these three?
First is the true mind, because it is free from discrimination.
Second is the mind of skillful means (*upāya-citta*), which spontaneously and universally acts for the benefit of sentient beings.
Third is the mind of karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna-citta*), which arises and ceases in a subtle manner.
Furthermore, when the Bodhisattva’s merits have reached full completion, he manifests a body that is the most sublime and vast in all worlds at the station of Akaniṣṭha.

That is to say, by means of wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, ignorance is suddenly exhausted; this is called the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Spontaneously, there arises inconceivable activity capable of manifesting throughout the ten directions to benefit sentient beings.

He asked: "Because space is limitless, worlds are limitless; because worlds are limitless, sentient beings are limitless; and because sentient beings are limitless, the distinctions in their mental activities are likewise limitless."
Such a realm is without boundaries, difficult to know and difficult to comprehend.
If ignorance is severed and no mental conceptions remain, how can it be fully understood? This is called the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
He replied:

"All objective realms are fundamentally the one mind, free from conceptualization. It is because sentient beings falsely perceive objective realms that the mind becomes limited; because they give rise to false conceptualizations that do not accord with the Dharma-nature, they are unable to reach definitive understanding."
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are free from views and perceptions and are omnipresent; because their minds are true and real, they are the very nature of all dharmas.

Their own essence illuminates all delusive phenomena, possessing the great function of wisdom and immeasurable skillful means. According to what each sentient being should understand, they are able to reveal various meanings of the Dharma; for this reason, they are named "Omniscient Wisdom" (sarvajñajñāna).
He asked again:

"If all Buddhas possess spontaneous karma (*anābhoga-karman*) that can manifest in all places to benefit sentient beings, then all sentient beings—whether they see their body, witness their spiritual transformations, or hear their teachings—will none fail to obtain benefit."
"Why is it that most in the world are unable to see it?
He replied,
"Because the Dharma-body of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas is equal and pervades all places, and is devoid of volitional effort."
Yet it is said that [the Tathāgata] is spontaneous, appearing solely in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
The mind of a sentient being is like a mirror; if the mirror is defiled by grime, reflections do not appear.
"In this way, if the minds of sentient beings possess defilements, the Dharma-body does not manifest.
Thus concludes the section on Exegesis.
Next is the section on Cultivating Faith in Practice.
In this context, for the sake of sentient beings who have not yet entered right concentration, the practice of faith is taught.
What is this faith?
How is it practiced?
Briefly stated, there are four kinds of faith.
What are the four?
First is faith in the root, which means delighting in mindfulness of the dharma of *tathatā* (suchness).

Second, they believe that the Buddha possesses immeasurable merit; they constantly mindfully approach, make offerings to, and revere him, thereby generating roots of goodness and aspiring for all-knowledge.
Third, they have faith that the Dharma brings great benefit, because they constantly mindfully practice the various pāramitās.

Fourth, they have faith that the Saṃgha is able to correctly practice for their own benefit and the benefit of others, because they always delight in drawing near to the assembly of bodhisattvas and seek to learn the practice of true realization.
There are five gates of practice that can bring this faith to fulfillment.
What are these five? First, the gate of giving; second, the gate of precepts; third, the gate of patience; fourth, the gate of diligence; and fifth, the gate of cessation and contemplation.
How does one practice the gate of giving?

If one sees anyone who comes seeking, one bestows whatever wealth and goods one possesses according to one's ability, thereby abandoning one's own stinginess and greed and causing the other to rejoice.
If one sees beings beset by calamity, terror, or peril, one should bestow fearlessness according to one's own capacity.
If there are sentient beings who come seeking the Dharma, one should explain it to them through skillful means according to what one understands.
One should not greedily seek fame, profit, or honor, but should instead contemplate only self-benefit and the benefit of others, dedicating all toward Bodhi.
How does one practice the gate of precepts? It is said:

not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not using double-tongued speech, not using harsh words, not speaking falsely, and not engaging in frivolous chatter; and remaining far removed from greed and envy, deception, flattery and crookedness, anger, and wrong views.

If one has gone forth from the household life, for the sake of subduing the afflictions, one should likewise distance oneself from bustle and noise, always dwell in tranquility, and cultivate practices such as fewness of desires, contentment, and the dhūta ascetic virtues.
One should feel dread even toward minor transgressions, feeling shame and remorse to reform and repent; one must not treat lightly the prohibitions and precepts established by the Tathāgata.
One should guard against censure and reproach so as not to cause sentient beings to give rise to false faults or offenses.
How does one practice the gate of patience?
It means that one should endure the provocations of others without harboring a desire for retaliation;
furthermore, one should likewise endure the eight worldly conditions: gain and loss, defamation and praise, fame and insignificance, suffering and pleasure.
What is the gateway to the practice of diligence?
It is that one’s mind does not slacken or retreat from any wholesome deeds, maintaining firm resolve and remaining free from cowardice or weakness.

One should reflect that since the distant past, one has pointlessly endured all manner of great physical and mental suffering without any benefit; therefore, one should diligently cultivate all meritorious virtues to benefit oneself and others, swiftly escaping all forms of suffering.

Furthermore, although a person may practice with faith, because they have accumulated many grave sins and karmic obstacles from previous lives, they may be harassed and disturbed by Māras, heterodox spirits, and various ghosts; or they may be entangled by the myriad affairs of the world; or they may be afflicted by the suffering of illness.

Because there are many such obstacles as these, one should therefore be courageous and diligent, worshipping the Buddhas during the six periods of the day and night, repenting with a sincere heart, requesting [the turning of the wheel of Dharma], rejoicing [in the merit of others], and dedicating [merit] toward Bodhi, never ceasing or abandoning this practice. By doing so, one will be able to escape all obstacles and cause one's roots of goodness to increase.
How does one practice the gateways of śamatha and vipaśyanā?
That which is called "stopping" (śamatha) refers to the cessation of all objective appearances, as it accords with the meaning of the contemplation of śamatha.

What is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā) refers to discerning the characteristics of arising and ceasing through causes and conditions, because it accords with the meaning of the contemplation of vipaśyanā.
How does it accord?
By means of these two meanings, one gradually cultivates them without separation, so that they both manifest together.

If one practices *śamatha*, one should dwell in a quiet place, sitting upright with right attention, not relying on inhalation or exhalation, not relying on forms or colors, not relying on space, not relying on earth, water, fire, or wind, and even not relying on seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.

All conceptualizations and recollections are eliminated, and even the thought of elimination is cast away, for all phenomena are originally signless; in every moment they are neither born nor extinguished. Furthermore, one does not follow the mind’s outward recollection of objects, subsequently using the mind to eliminate the mind.
If the mind wanders and scatters, one should immediately collect it and abide in right mindfulness.
Regarding this right mindfulness, one should know that there is only mind and no external objects.

Furthermore, this very mind has no self-characteristic; it cannot be apprehended in any single thought-moment. Whether rising from one's seat, going or coming, advancing or stopping, or performing any other action, at all times one should constantly maintain skillful means and observe accordingly. Through long-term practice until it is thoroughly matured, the mind will attain stability.

Because the mind abides [in this state], it gradually becomes sharp and intense; accordingly, one enters the samādhi of suchness, deeply subdues afflictions, increases in faith, and swiftly achieves the stage of non-retrogression.
Except for those who harbor doubt, lack faith, slander, have committed grave offenses, possess karmic obstructions, are arrogant, or are indolent—such people as these are unable to enter.
Furthermore, by relying on such samādhi, one knows that the dharma-realm has a single characteristic.
That is to say, the dharma-body of all Buddhas and the bodies of sentient beings are equal and non-dual; this is called the Samādhi of Single Practice.
One should know that suchness is the root of samādhi; if a person practices it, they will gradually be able to give rise to immeasurable samādhis.

There may be sentient beings who lack the power of roots of goodness and are thus deluded and disturbed by various māras, externalists, and spirits, who may manifest terrifying forms or the appearances of handsome men and women while one is seated in meditation. One should then contemplate that these are but the mind alone; the objective realm will then vanish, and one will ultimately not be troubled by them.

He may manifest the form of a deva or a bodhisattva, or likewise manifest the form of a Tathāgata complete with all the primary and secondary marks.
