He may preach dhāraṇīs, or preach generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; or he may preach equality, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the absence of enmity and the absence of kinship, the absence of cause and the absence of effect, and that ultimate emptiness and quiescence is true nirvāṇa.

Or they may cause people to know matters of past lives and also know future events; they may attain the knowledge of others' minds and unimpeded eloquence, thereby causing sentient beings to become greedily attached to worldly fame and profit.
Furthermore, it causes those they employ to become frequently angry and frequently joyful, their natures lacking any constant standard.
They may become excessively compassionate, prone to sleep, or frequently ill, their minds becoming indolent.
Or they may suddenly exert great diligence only to later abandon and neglect it, giving rise to a lack of faith and becoming full of doubt and excessive deliberation.
Alternatively, one may abandon fundamental superior practices to cultivate miscellaneous karmas;

or, if one becomes attached to worldly affairs and is entangled by various distractions, this can also cause a person to attain a semblance of various samādhis. All such states are obtained by non-Buddhists and are not true samādhi.

Furthermore, it may cause a person to remain in meditative concentration for one day, two days, three days, or even up to seven days, obtaining naturally fragrant and delicious food and drink; their body and mind become so refreshed and joyful that they feel neither hunger nor thirst, causing them to become attached.
Or it may cause a person to eat without moderation, such that their intake fluctuates between much and little, and their complexion changes.
For this reason, a practitioner should always observe with wisdom so as not to allow this mind to fall into the net of error.
One should diligently maintain right mindfulness, neither grasping nor clinging; thus, one can remain far removed from these various karmic obstructions.
You should know that all the samādhis of the non-Buddhists do not transcend the mind of views, craving, and self-conceit, for they are greedily attached to worldly fame, profit, and honor.

As for the samādhi of suchness, one does not dwell on the mark of seeing nor the mark of attainment; even upon emerging from concentration, there is no indolence or arrogance, and all afflictions gradually become thin and faint.
If ordinary beings do not practice this dharma of samādhi, it is impossible for them to enter the lineage of the Tathāgatas.

This is because their cultivation of worldly meditations and samādhis mostly gives rise to attachment to their flavor; relying on the view of self, they remain bound to the three realms and share [these states] with non-Buddhists.
If one is separated from the protection of virtuous friends, one will give rise to the views of non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, those who diligently and single-mindedly practice and study this samādhi shall obtain ten kinds of benefits in the present life.
What are the ten?
First, they are constantly protected and remembered by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
Second, they cannot be terrified by any demons or malevolent spirits.
Third, they will not be deluded or disturbed by the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist paths, ghosts, or spirits.
Fourth, they will distance themselves from the grave offense of slandering the profound Dharma, and their karmic obstructions will gradually become thin and slight.
Fifth, they extinguish all doubts and all evil discursive thoughts.
Sixth, their faith in the realm of the Tathāgata increases.
Seventh, they remain free from sorrow and regret, remaining courageous and undaunted amidst the cycle of birth and death.
Eighth, his mind is gentle and supple; having abandoned arrogance, he is not troubled by others.
Ninth, although he has not yet attained meditative concentration, at all times and in all circumstances, he is able to diminish his afflictions and takes no pleasure in the world.
Tenth: if one attains samādhi, one will not be startled or disturbed by any external sounds or conditions.

Furthermore, if a person practices only *śamatha*, the mind may become sunken or indolent; one will take no delight in various virtues and remain distant from great compassion. For this reason, one must practice *vipaśyanā*.

One who practices contemplation should observe that all conditioned phenomena in the world cannot endure for long but undergo change and decay in an instant; all mental activities arise and perish from moment to moment, and for this reason, they are suffering.

One should contemplate all phenomena contemplated in the past as being as insubstantial and fleeting as a dream; one should contemplate all phenomena contemplated in the present as being like flashes of lightning; one should contemplate all phenomena contemplated in the future as being like clouds that suddenly arise; and one should contemplate all embodied beings in the world as entirely impure, defiled by various kinds of filth, such that not a single one is worth desiring.
One should reflect in this way:

"All sentient beings, from beginningless time until now, have had their minds undergo arising and ceasing due to being permeated by ignorance; consequently, they have already undergone all manner of great suffering of body and mind."

In the present, there are already immeasurable oppressions, and the sufferings of the future are likewise boundless; yet beings find it difficult to relinquish or depart from them, remaining unaware of their plight.
Such are sentient beings, and they are truly to be pitied.
Having formed this reflection, one should immediately establish a great vow with vigor:

"May my mind, free from conceptual discrimination, cultivate all virtuous merits throughout the ten directions until the end of the future; and by means of immeasurable skillful expedients, may I rescue and deliver all suffering sentient beings, enabling them to attain the ultimate bliss of Nirvāṇa."

Because he has aroused such a vow, at all times and in all places, he practices and cultivates all forms of goodness according to his capacity without forsaking them; his mind is free from indolence, except when he is seated and single-mindedly focused on *śamatha*.
If there is anything else whatsoever, one should examine in every case whether it should be done or not.
Whether walking or standing, lying down or rising, one should always practice both śamatha and vipaśyanā together.

This means that although one contemplates that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unborn, one simultaneously contemplates that through the conjunction of causes and conditions, the karma of good and evil and its retributions of suffering and pleasure are neither lost nor destroyed.
Although one contemplates the causes and conditions of the retribution of good and evil karma, one simultaneously realizes that their intrinsic nature is ungraspable.
If one practices *śamatha*, it serves as an antidote to the ordinary person’s attachment to the mundane world and enables one to relinquish the timid views of the two vehicles.

If one practices contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), it serves as an antidote to the fault of the two vehicles’ failure to give rise to great compassion and their narrow-mindedness, while distancing one from the ordinary person’s failure to cultivate roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
For this reason, these two gates of calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) mutually assist and complete one another, never being separated.
If one lacks both tranquility (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā), one will be unable to enter the path to Bodhi.
Furthermore, when sentient beings first study this Dharma and seek to attain right faith, their minds become timid and weak.
Because they dwell in this Sahā world, they fear that they may not always encounter the Buddhas to personally receive them and make offerings;
fearing that their faith might be difficult to perfect and intending to retreat, they should know that the Tathāgata possesses supreme skillful means to protect and sustain their faith.

This means that by virtue of the causal conditions of single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha, one will be born in a buddha-land of another direction according to one's vow, constantly seeing the Buddha and forever departing from the evil realms.

As stated in the sutras: "If a person single-mindedly recollects Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, and dedicates their cultivated roots of goodness with the vow to seek birth in that world, they shall immediately attain birth there; because they constantly see the Buddha, they shall never fall back."

If one contemplates that Buddha’s *tathatā-dharmakāya* and constantly and diligently practices [this contemplation], one will ultimately attain birth [therein], because one abides in right concentration (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
This concludes the section on the cultivation of faith.
Next, the section on the benefits of exhorting others to practice is explained.
Thus, I have provided a general exposition of this Mahāyāna, the secret treasury of all Buddhas.

If there are sentient beings who wish to give rise to right faith regarding the profound realm of the Tathāgata, to remain far removed from slander, and to enter the path of the Mahāyāna, they should uphold this treatise, contemplate it, and cultivate its practice; in the end, they will be able to reach the unsurpassed way.

If a person, having heard this Dharma, does not give rise to cowardice or weakness, you should know that this person will certainly succeed to the lineage of the Buddhas and will surely receive the prediction of enlightenment from all the Buddhas.

Even if someone were able to transform all sentient beings filling a trichiliocosm so that they practice the ten wholesome paths of action, it would not equal a person who, for the duration of a single meal, correctly contemplates this Dharma; the latter’s merit surpasses the former beyond all comparison.
Furthermore, if a person upholds this treatise and observes its practice for even a single day and night, the resulting merit will be immeasurable, boundless, and beyond description.
Even if all the Buddhas of the ten directions were each to praise his merits for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they would still be unable to exhaust them.
Why is this? It is because the qualities of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) are inexhaustible.
The merit of this person is likewise thus, having no limit.

If there are sentient beings who, within this treatise, slander it and do not believe in it, they will receive a retribution of sin such that they shall undergo great suffering and affliction for immeasurable kalpas.

Therefore, sentient beings should simply have reverent faith and should not engage in disparagement; for by doing so, they deeply harm themselves as well as others, severing the seeds of the Triple Gem, since all Tathāgatas attain nirvāṇa by relying on this Dharma, and all Bodhisattvas enter the Buddha-wisdom by means of its practice.

One should know that past bodhisattvas have already attained pure faith by relying on this Dharma; present bodhisattvas are now attaining pure faith by relying on this Dharma; and future bodhisattvas shall attain pure faith by relying on this Dharma. Therefore, sentient beings should diligently practice and study it.
The profound and vast meaning of all Buddhas, I now recite in its entirety according to my capacity;
may this merit, like the nature of reality (dharmatā), universally benefit the entire realm of sentient beings.
The Treatise on the Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna, One Scroll.
